title: Trait objects: values of different types
summary: The GUI example, dyn Trait behind a pointer, generics versus trait objects, static and dynamic dispatch, vtables and fat pointers, dyn compatibility rules, downcasting with Any, and supertraits.

sections: TRPL 18.2 Using Trait Objects to Abstract over Shared Behavior
TRPL 18.2 Defining a Trait for Common Behavior
TRPL 18.2 Trait Objects and Type Inference
PR ch11 Generic Functions vs Trait Objects

blocks.md:
A vector holds one type. But sometimes a collection must hold **different** types that share behavior: a GUI library draws buttons, text fields and images, and users of the library will add types the library authors never saw. With an enum you must list every variant up front. With **trait objects** you do not.

*The Rust Programming Language* sketches such a library. Everything on screen implements a `Draw` trait, and a `Screen` keeps a list of things to draw:

blocks.explain: `Box<dyn Draw>` reads "a box holding some type that implements `Draw`". The `Screen` never learns the concrete types. In the book, `draw` returns nothing and would paint on screen; here it returns text so you can see the result.

blocks.title: dyn Trait
blocks.md:
A **trait object** is written `dyn Trait`. It always sits **behind a pointer**: `&dyn Draw`, `Box<dyn Draw>`, `Rc<dyn Draw>`. The pointer is needed because different implementing types have different sizes, and a value of unknown size cannot live directly in a variable or a vector slot.

Compare with a generic version:

```rust
pub struct Screen<T: Draw> {
    pub components: Vec<T>,
}
```

This compiles too, but a `Screen<Button>` can hold **only** buttons. Generics fix one type per use; trait objects allow a mix at run time.

blocks.title: Generics or trait objects?
rows: **static**: the method is chosen at compile time

blocks.title: Dynamic dispatch: what is inside a &dyn Draw

steps.title: A fat pointer
steps.md: A `&dyn Draw` is two machine words: a pointer to the data, and a pointer to a **vtable** (virtual method table) for the concrete type. `Box<dyn Draw>` is the same, with ownership.

steps.title: One vtable per (type, trait) pair
steps.md: The compiler generates a table for each type used as that trait object: the size and alignment of the type, its `drop` function, and a pointer to each trait method.
steps.code:
VTable for Button as Draw:
    size, align, drop_in_place::<Button>,
    draw: <Button as Draw>::draw

steps.title: Calling a method
steps.md: `component.draw()` loads the `draw` entry from the vtable and calls it with the data pointer as `self`. That is one extra memory load and an indirect call, which also prevents inlining.

steps.title: *Rust in Action*'s view
steps.md: A trait object trades a little speed for flexibility. In most programs the cost is negligible; in a hot inner loop, prefer generics.

blocks.explain: Like a slice reference (address and length), a trait object reference is a fat pointer (address and vtable).

blocks.title: Dyn compatibility
blocks.md:
Not every trait can be used as `dyn Trait`. The compiler must be able to build a vtable, so the trait must be **dyn compatible** (formerly called *object safe*). The main rules for each method:

- it must not return `Self` (the concrete type is unknown, so its size is unknown);
- it must not have generic type parameters (a vtable cannot hold infinitely many copies).

`Clone` breaks the first rule (`fn clone(&self) -> Self`), so `Box<dyn Clone>` is an error. A method can opt out with `where Self: Sized`: it then is not callable on trait objects, but the rest of the trait is.

blocks.output:
error[E0038]: the trait `Clone` is not dyn compatible

  = note: the trait is not dyn compatible because it requires `Self: Sized`

blocks.title: Supertraits and downcasting
blocks.md:
A trait can require another: `trait Shape: Debug { ... }` means every `Shape` is also `Debug`, so a `&dyn Shape` can be printed with `{:?}`. This is a **supertrait**, *Programming Rust*'s "subtrait" relationship.

Sometimes you need the concrete type back from a trait object. **`std::any::Any`** supports that: `Box<dyn Any>` can be `downcast::<T>()`, returning `Ok(Box<T>)` if the value really is a `T`. Needing it often is a sign that an enum would fit better.

blocks.title: A plugin list
blocks.md: Write a `Plugin` trait with `fn name(&self) -> String` and `fn run(&self, input: i64) -> i64`. Implement it for `Double` and for `AddN(i64)`, put them in a `Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>>`, and run the input through every plugin in order, printing each step.
hints: `trait Plugin { fn name(&self) -> String; fn run(&self, input: i64) -> i64; }`
`vec![Box::new(Double), Box::new(AddN(7)), Box::new(Double)]` with the type annotation `Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>>`.

blocks.title: A shape registry
blocks.goal: Store different types behind dyn Trait, use a supertrait, and know when generics are the better tool.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub trait Shape: std::fmt::Debug { fn area(&self) -> f64; fn name(&self) -> &'static str; fn scale(&mut self, k: f64); }`.
- Implement it for `pub struct Circle { pub r: f64 }` (`"circle"`) and `pub struct Rect { pub w: f64, pub h: f64 }` (`"rect"`), both deriving `Debug`.
- `pub struct Registry { shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> }` with `new`, `pub fn add(&mut self, s: Box<dyn Shape>)`, `pub fn total_area(&self) -> f64`, `pub fn largest(&self) -> Option<&dyn Shape>` (the first on a tie), `pub fn scale_all(&mut self, k: f64)` and `pub fn count_by_name(&self, name: &str) -> usize`.
- A **generic** helper `pub fn sum_areas<T: Shape>(items: &[T]) -> f64` for slices of one type (static dispatch).

examples.input: registry with Circle { r: 1.0 } and Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 }: total_area()

hints: `scale` for a circle multiplies `r` by `k`; for a rect, both sides (so the area grows by `k * k`).
`largest`: iterate and keep the reference with the bigger area; return `Some(best.as_ref())` (`&Box<dyn Shape>` → `&dyn Shape`).
blocks.solution_explain: The registry mixes circles and rectangles, so it needs `dyn Shape`. `sum_areas` takes a slice of one type, so a generic is the better fit: static dispatch, inlinable. `Debug` as a supertrait lets you print any `&dyn Shape`.

questions.q: Why must `dyn Trait` be behind a pointer like `Box` or `&`?
options: Different implementing types have different sizes, so the size of dyn Trait is unknown
Traits are always on the heap
questions.explanation: A pointer has a fixed size.

options: A per-type table of method pointers used for dynamic dispatch
questions.explanation: The trait object's second pointer points to it.

options: `clone` returns Self, whose size is unknown behind a trait object

points: `dyn Trait` behind a pointer holds any type implementing the trait; collections can mix types.
Trait objects use dynamic dispatch through a vtable; generics use static dispatch.
A `&dyn Trait` is a fat pointer: data plus vtable.
Only dyn compatible traits can be trait objects: no methods returning `Self` or with generic parameters.
Supertraits add requirements (`trait Shape: Debug`); `Any` allows downcasting when truly needed.

terms.def: A value of type dyn Trait behind a pointer, standing for any type that implements the trait.
Choosing which method implementation to call at run time, through a vtable.
Choosing the method at compile time, as with generics.
A table of function pointers for one type's implementation of a trait.
A trait that can be made into a trait object (formerly object safe).
A trait required by another trait, as in trait Shape: Debug.
